costRanges.item: Hidden-rot re-deck added during a re-roof
costRanges.source: Refined Home Services / HomeHero (contractor cost data)

costRanges.item: NJ premium over national figures (labor ~60% of repair total)

signs: Daylight visible through the roof deck from inside the attic (a direct breach in the sheathing that points toward replacement, not a surface patch)
Soft, spongy, or crumbling wood underfoot or to a probe (significant decay; moisture-rotted sheathing loses the ability to hold a roofing nail and reduces wind resistance)
A deck that sags between the rafters (moisture-decayed sheathing or undersized panels)
Delaminated plywood layers or swollen OSB edges (sheathing past recovery)
Dark stains or mold on the deck underside seen from the attic (trapped moisture decaying the sheathing, preceding lost fastener hold)
Water-soaked decking exposed at tear-off during a re-roof (must be removed before re-covering)

technicalFacts.fact: The roof deck is the plywood or OSB sheathing that spans the rafters; it is the structural substrate that anchors every roofing nail and carries the underlayment and the covering.

Roofing nails must penetrate at least 3/4 inch (19 mm) into the deck, or fully through plus 1/8 inch (3 mm) where the deck is under 3/4 inch thick, so the deck must grip the fastener; sheathing that cannot grip a nail must be replaced.
Asphalt-shingle nails are corrosion-resistant with at least a 12-gauge (0.105 in) shank and a 3/8-inch head.
Trapped moisture decays the sheathing until the deck loses the ability to hold a fastener and the roof loses wind resistance.

Plywood is cross-laminated, dries more uniformly, and partly recovers after wetting; OSB swells at the edges and delaminates irreversibly once saturated, so saturated OSB is re-decked rather than dried out.

Wood structural sheathing carries an APA span rating that sets the maximum rafter spacing: 7/16-inch panels rate 24/16, 15/32-inch panels 32/16, 19/32-inch panels 40/20, and 23/32-inch panels 48/24 (the first number is the max rafter spacing for roof use); 7/16-inch is the typical code minimum at 16-24 inch o.c.
InterNACHI's min-thickness guidance cites 5/8 inch at 24-inch rafter spacing (more conservative than APA's 7/16-inch code minimum).

Repair or replacement of the roof covering on a detached one- and two-family dwelling is ordinary maintenance requiring no construction permit, inspection, or notice; a structural change to rafters or trusses still triggers a permit.
On a commercial building, repairing more than 25% of the total roof area within a 12-month period requires a permit.
Contractor-consensus thresholds: replace the roof when damage exceeds 25-30% of the roof area or when one repair approaches 50% of replacement cost; otherwise repair localized decay.

codes.requirement: Reroofing provisions prohibit roofing over a water-soaked or deteriorated deck; the unsound sheathing must be removed or repaired before re-covering.
Wood structural panels thinner than 1/2 inch over rafters spaced more than 20 inches on center require H-clips, tongue-and-groove edges, or solid blocking.
Self-adhering ice barrier runs from the eave to at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line (36 inches up-slope on roofs 8:12 or steeper, still in force under the 2021 IRC adopted in NJ).
Roof-covering repair/replacement on a detached 1-2 family dwelling is ordinary maintenance (no permit); commercial repair of more than 25% of roof area in 12 months requires a permit.

defabToKill.issue: Intro frames 'inadequate ventilation' as a cause that 'allowed moisture to reach the deck,' implying ventilation deficit is a primary moisture/ice-dam driver.
defabToKill.fix: Per Building Science Digest 135 / Univ. of Minnesota Extension, ice-dam and condensation moisture trace to attic heat loss / air leakage from the living space; ventilation contributes to prevention but is not the primary root cause. Frame deck decay as driven by trapped moisture (failed flashing, clogged gutters overflowing the eave, attic condensation) per InterNACHI.

defabToKill.issue: 'During NJ snow events, the additional weight on already compromised sheathing creates real risk of localized collapse' is unsourced alarmist speculation.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the collapse claim. Use the grounded mechanism: rotted/sagging sheathing loses the ability to hold a roofing nail and reduces the roof's wind resistance, per InterNACHI; IRC R908 prohibits roofing over a deteriorated deck.

defabToKill.issue: No named sources cited anywhere in the article (every sign asserted bare).
defabToKill.fix: Attribute each sign: daylight breach / soft-spongy wood / sag / delamination / underside staining per InterNACHI and GAF inspection guidance; the fastener-hold mechanism per ARMA; the no-recover rule per IRC R908.

defabToKill.issue: '$75-150 per 4x8 panel' for spot deck repair contradicts the gold/contractor source.
defabToKill.fix: Use $50-$120 per 4-by-8 sheet for a hidden-rot re-deck added during a re-roof, per Refined Home Services / HomeHero contractor cost data.

defabToKill.issue: Invented whole-project totals '$225-1,500' (3-10 panels), '$1,500-4,000' (20+ panels) with no named source.
defabToKill.fix: Remove invented panel-count totals. The gold gives only per-square-foot and per-sheet pricing with named sources; pair $2-$5/sq ft (HomeGuide, avg ~$5,500) and $2-$6/sq ft (Angi) and the $50-$120/sheet add-on with free-written-estimate framing.

defabToKill.issue: 'CDX plywood at $35-50 per 4x8 sheet' and 'OSB at $20-35 per sheet' material prices are unsourced and lower than the fact pack.
defabToKill.fix: Use OSB ~$20-$50 vs roofing-grade plywood ~$50-$80 per 4-by-8 sheet, per Colony Roofers / Fixr / Angi; OSB costs less than plywood per sheet.

defabToKill.issue: Calls plywood 'premium' and asserts plywood 'dries faster and retains more strength' / OSB 'performs adequately' as bare opinion.
defabToKill.fix: Keep it qualitative and sourced: plywood dries more uniformly and partly recovers after wetting, while OSB swells at the edges and delaminates irreversibly once saturated, per InterNACHI and trade guidance. Both carry an APA span rating and either grips a nail at least 3/4 inch deep per ARMA.

defabToKill.issue: 'NJ building code requires minimum 7/16-inch OSB or 1/2-inch plywood... at 16 in o.c.; for 24-inch spacing increases to 5/8-inch' presents these as NJ code minimums.
defabToKill.fix: Reframe via the APA span-rating system (7/16=24/16, 15/32=32/16, 19/32=40/20, 23/32=48/24, per APA): the first number is the max rafter spacing. The 5/8-inch-at-24-inch figure is InterNACHI guidance (more conservative than APA's code minimum), NOT a code minimum. The enforceable code rule is IRC R803.2: panels under 1/2 inch over rafters over 20 inches o.c. need H-clips/T&G/blocking.

defabToKill.issue: 'more than 25% of the roof area... NJ municipalities may require a building permit' applied loosely to residential re-decking.
defabToKill.fix: Residential roof-covering replacement (incl. re-decking exposed at tear-off) on a detached 1-2 family dwelling is ordinary maintenance with no permit under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7; the >25%-in-12-months permit threshold is the COMMERCIAL rule. A structural change to rafters/trusses triggers a permit.

defabToKill.issue: 'Essex County's humid climate and 80+ freeze-thaw cycles per winter' is an invented, unsourced statistic.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the fabricated cycle count. Keep the grounded mechanism: trapped moisture (failed flashing, clogged gutters overflowing the eave, attic condensation) decays sheathing per InterNACHI; ice-dam moisture roots in attic heat loss / air leakage, not ventilation alone (Building Science Digest 135 / Univ. of Minnesota Extension).

defabToKill.issue: 'Full deck overlay adds $3,000-6,000 to a re-roof but creates a new structural platform for 30+ years' — invented whole-project total + invented deck lifespan, both unsourced.
defabToKill.fix: Remove the $3,000-$6,000 total and the '30+ years' deck-lifespan number (deck-specific lifespan is on the banned list). Use the sourced per-sq-ft / per-sheet re-decking costs and free-estimate framing; full re-deck is warranted when damage exceeds the 25-30% area threshold (contractor consensus) or the deck is below code thickness.

defabToKill.issue: 'price savings of $10-15 per panel' between OSB and plywood is an unsourced fabricated figure.
defabToKill.fix: State the sourced spread instead: OSB ~$20-$50 vs roofing-grade plywood ~$50-$80 per 4-by-8 sheet, per Colony Roofers / Fixr / Angi.

defabToKill.issue: 'controlled factory manufacturing of OSB delivers consistent structural properties that plywood's natural wood variation cannot match' and 'insurance value of plywood's resilience' are unsupported marketing claims.
defabToKill.fix: Hold to sourced facts: both panels carry an APA span rating that sets max rafter spacing (APA); plywood dries more uniformly and partly recovers while OSB delaminates once saturated (InterNACHI/trade); OSB costs less per sheet. Frame plywood vs OSB as a moisture-resilience-vs-cost tradeoff without inventing superiority claims.

articleAngles.signs: Answer that the deck needs repair/replacement when sheathing shows daylight breaches, soft/spongy/crumbling wood, sag between rafters, delaminated plywood or swollen OSB edges, or underside staining/mold; the strongest grounded facts are the six InterNACHI/GAF inspection signs, the ARMA fastener-hold mechanism (rot = no nail grip = lost wind resistance), and the IRC R908 no-recover-over-deteriorated-deck rule. Frame moisture sources as failed flashing / overflowing gutters / attic condensation (not ventilation as primary cause).
articleAngles.costGuide: Answer that NJ re-decking runs $2-$5 per square foot (HomeGuide, avg ~$5,500) or $2-$6 per square foot (Angi), with a hidden-rot re-deck added during a re-roof at about $50-$120 per 4-by-8 sheet (Refined Home Services / HomeHero); OSB ~$20-$50 vs roofing-grade plywood ~$50-$80 per sheet (Colony Roofers / Fixr / Angi); NJ sits 10-40% above national figures with labor ~60% of the total (Integrity Home Exteriors). No whole-project dollar total exists in the gold, so close with a free-written-estimate CTA and cite the APA span-rating thickness rule, not invented panel-count subtotals.
articleAngles.decision: Answer the broad overview: the deck is the plywood/OSB sheathing that anchors every roofing nail (ARMA 3/4-inch penetration), it decays from trapped moisture (InterNACHI), and replace vs repair turns on extent — replace localized panels for limited decay, re-deck when damage exceeds the 25-30% contractor-consensus area threshold or the deck is below APA-rated code thickness. Cover the APA span-rating thickness system, IRC R803.2 panel/H-clip rule, IRC R908 no-recover rule, plywood-vs-OSB moisture tradeoff (InterNACHI), and the NJ permit split (residential ordinary maintenance vs commercial >25%/12-mo, N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7). Verification points: confirm the deck grips a nail before re-covering and get a free written estimate that specifies panels by APA span rating.
